newsitem.title: JAPAN: Relieved dollar heads higher in brief Tokyo rally.
newsitem.headline: Relieved dollar heads higher in brief Tokyo rally.

text.p: The dollar rallied briefly in Tokyo on Wednesday on U.S. election results that showed the Republicans heading for control of both houses of Congress, and it could go higher still, dealers and analysts said.
But with the results, including the re-election of incumbent President Bill Clinton, basically as expected, the immediate impact was due more to a sense of relief than anything else.

"There is a sense that this will be maintaining the status quo in terms of policy, and also maintaining the push to bring down the budget deficit," said Kenneth Landon, senior currency strategist at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell in Tokyo.
Currency dealers agreed, saying the apparent Republican majority in both the U.S. Senate and House of Representatives reconfirmed overseas investors' confidence in American assets.

"Since yesterday, the currency market has not been too concerned about the presidential contest, which Clinton won as expected. It's the congressional elections that they've been watching most," said Yasuhito Kawashima, chief manager in foreign exchange at Toyo Trust & Banking Co Ltd.
The dollar had risen by noon on confirmation of the Republican majority in the Senate, but surged even more in early afternoon as expectations of the Republican House victory strengthened.

It briefly touched a high of 114.40 yen before pressure from profit-taking sales forced it lower. By 0600 GMT the dollar was around 114.30 yen against its Tuesday close of around 114.22 yen in New York.

The Republicans kept the Senate by winning open seats previously held by Democrats in Alabama, Nebraska and President Bill Clinton's home state of Arkansas. That guaranteed them at least 51 seats in the 100-seat chamber.
Television projections also said the House of Representatives would remain in Republican hands.
Deutsche Morgan Grenfell's Landon said he expected the results to boost the greenback eventually, but that it could well undergo a bit of consolidation and downward correction over the coming weeks.

"All the good news is out now and there won't be much in the way of factors for the market to trade on now," he said, adding that large dollar slides are unlikely as Japanese operators will be eager to buy on any dips.
U.S. Treasury bonds also rose, mainly on news of the likely Republican congressional victory, and dealers said this was expected to give the dollar some additional support.
